extracted.intended_audience: Press Gazette journalists, editors and contributors (news writers)
extracted.subtask_description: House style and usage rules for writing news and features for Press Gazette, covering grammar, punctuation, attribution, formatting, banned words and newsroom practice. Primarily for internal use by journalists and sub-editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations, contractions and acronyms do not take full points (so use “eg”, “etc” and “ie”). Spell out the names of organisations in full in the first instance: National Union of Journalists, then NUJ; Independent Press Standards Organisation, then IPSO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accents and foreign words and phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use accents consistently in foreign words and names. Commonly used words and phrases go in Roman type (with accents where necessary): ad lib, angst, avant-garde, cliché, coup, crudité, en masse, en route, et al, kitsch, pro rata, realpolitik.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using phrases where there are two spellings that correspond to gender, always use the version that denotes the correct gender (fiancé(e), protégé(e), alumnus/alumna, doyen(ne)). Use correct plurals (bureaux, cadeaux, chateaux).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: All facts which we are not absolutely certain to be true should be attributed – with links where possible. Even if this is to “a well-placed source”. Never make statements of fact without attribution unless we know for certain that they are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering surveys, legal judgments and reports – always link through to the full report where possible. Taking possibly disputable facts from other sources without attribution is plagiarism and dangerous because we cannot explain their origin if challenged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bullet points style
rubrics_metrics.description: The style for bullet points is as follows: First item on list / second item on list / third item on list / and so on / to the last one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: So we treat the bullet itself as the punctuation between each item.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: We treat collective nouns, corporate bodies and institutions (such as the government, unions, Labour, any company) as singular — thus, “Marks & Spencer is well known”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political parties are singular in full form (the Conservative Party is) but may be plural in informal shortenings (the Lib Dems are, the Tories are).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Date style is “Thursday 3 April 1997”, “3 April 1997” and “the 3 April election” (no commas). For a range use “15-20 November 2007”. Write 'the 1970s' (no apostrophe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use “1995-96”, not “1995-6” or “1995/96”; but use “2001-2002” (not “2001-2”). Use appropriate full ranges for centuries or small spans (eg, “1001-1010”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics and capitalised words
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid italics for emphasis in text except where absolutely necessary. Avoid using capital letters for emphasis except where absolutely necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location references
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume everyone knows that a location is in London. Spell it out. So, for example, “Camden, north London”.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers (general rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers one to ten are spelled out. Use figures for 11 upwards; exceptions include “eleven-plus” and vague approximations (about a hundred people). Ages follow the same rule; use 'in their twenties' etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinals spelled out from “first” to “tenth”; use figures from 11th upwards (exception: “at the eleventh hour”). Spell out 'part one' but use 'page 7'. Spell out numerals at sentence start or avoid starting with a numeral. Use figures with units (5mm, 1p). Use numerals with 'per cent' — '6 per cent' (never 6% except tables/sidebars). Decimalise simple fractions (3.5) and round complicated fractions to one decimal (3.3) unless precision is necessary. Use commas in figures over three digits (1,000). Use 'first, second and third' not 'firstly' etc. Age: 'a six-year-old girl' or 'she was six years old'. Currency: abbreviate million/billion (no final 's'): '£5m', '£4bn' and decimalise ('£1.5m'). Time: use 12-hour clock with 'am'/'pm' closed up (4am, 7pm, 12.30pm), but write '12 noon' and '12 midnight'. In percentages, decimalise fractions when simple; avoid complicated fractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Off the record / background / confidential sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Before publishing any information based on 'off the record' interviews, clarify exactly what the terms are under which that information can be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If information is shared confidentially we agree to keep it secret until the source agrees to go public. 'Background' means we can use the information but without quotes or attribution (only if certain it is correct). If we can quote but not name the source, clarify how they should be described: 'a company source', 'a well-placed source', 'a source close to...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per cent usage
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Per cent’ is spelled out except if space needed for a headline (especially online).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always use numbers rather than words in front of 'per cent' (eg, '3 per cent').

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophes
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a name or proper noun ends in 's' use ’s to denote possession, eg, 'Tom Jones’s book'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas
rubrics_metrics.description: Use commas sparingly. Where the order of a sentence is clear, you may dispense with them: 'She thought about it and then decided to send her a letter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use commas rather than dashes where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colons and semi-colons
rubrics_metrics.description: The semicolon links equal or balanced clauses, the colon generally marks a step forward, from introduction to main theme, from cause to effect, premise to conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Always remember before you cross a road: look both ways.' Use semi-colons sparingly and avoid them in news stories if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation and dashes
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate nouns when used as compound adjectives: 'three-year course', 'part-time job', 'short-term trend', 'middle-class woman'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep hyphenation to a minimum (use 'trade union source' not 'trade-union source'). Triple-barrelled hyphenation is possible but avoid where possible. Do not hyphenate adverbial phrases ending in '-ly' (a beautifully furnished house).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use double quotation marks (single marks for quotations within quotations). Use square brackets [ ] for an editorial addition to a quotation. Use an ellipsis ( . . . ) for an omission from a quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punctuation: where a complete sentence is quoted, put the full-stop inside the quotation marks; where a partial sentence is quoted, the stop should be outside. Examples (a–h) demonstrate placement and use of brackets/commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show don't tell
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid telling readers that things are 'shocking', 'stunning', 'extraordinary' etc.; let facts and the story speak for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use qualifiers like 'only' or 'just' to downplay numbers (eg, don't say 'only six out of ten'). Let speakers in quotes express shock or emphasis rather than the writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: That / Which
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally prefer 'that' but use 'which' after a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'This is the house that Jack built.' vs 'The house, which Jack built, is covered in stucco.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles and names
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using Ms, Miss, Mr, Mrs, Dr and so on. Use forename and surname at the first mention. Thereafter use the surname only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred constructions: 'Daily Mail editor Paul Dacre said:' rather than 'Daily Mail editor, Paul Dacre, said:' or 'Paul Dacre, editor of the Daily Mail, said:'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper and lower case rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed rules on when to use capitals: Acts and bills take initial caps when referring to a specific title ('Mental Health Act 1967') but 'the act' is lower case. Books, magazines and newspapers: no italics. Brand names initial caps but prefer generic alternatives where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree classifications: First, (Upper) Second, Third. Empires usually lower case ('British empire'). Geographic regions: 'East End', 'West End' but 'west of London'. Government generally lower case (except current UK Government); select committees take upper case when using the full title ('Commons Foreign Affairs Select Committee'). For the US, 'Senate', 'House of Representatives' and 'Congress' are capped; 'senator' and 'congressman' are lower case unless part of a name. British government departments use 'Department for/Ministry of...', thereafter 'the department' or DfE/DfID, and 'the Treasury'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words to watch out for (preferred spellings/usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: List of words/spellings to prefer: adviser (not advisor), alright (not allright), bi-monthly (specify meaning), crowdfunded (one word), defuse (not diffuse), discreet vs discrete distinctions, dispatch not despatch, email, fewer vs less, focused, inquiry not enquiry, internet (lowercase), judgment not judgement for legal cases, sceptic (not skeptic), sub-editor, tabloid (rather than compact), website (one word), whistle-blower, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also notes on odd proper names/spellings (eg, Kelvin MacKenzie but his brother Colin Mackenzie).

rubrics_metrics.name: The banned list
rubrics_metrics.description: Words and phrases the paper avoids using (banned or discouraged): 'cancer battles', 'cheating death', 'CEO' (use chief executive), 'delighted' (as in 'I’m delighted to announce...'), 'extraordinary', 'got', 'hack' (as synonym for journalist), 'hits out' (sometimes unavoidable in headlines), 'mystery surrounds', 'raft' (unless literal), 'really', 'Revealed:' (as a headline kicker online), 'recently', 'very', 'slams' (unless for doors), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some banned items may be acceptable in print for space or in unavoidable contexts; online writing should avoid these. Preference is to use clearer, more precise language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of newspapers (masthead form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use names of newspapers as they appear on the masthead (listed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: Daily Express, Daily Mail, Daily Mirror, Daily Record, Daily Star, Daily Star Sunday, Financial Times, The Independent on Sunday, News of the World, Racing Post, Scotland on Sunday, Sunday Express, Sunday Herald, Sunday Mail, Sunday Mirror, Sunday People, Sunday Post, The Daily Telegraph, The Guardian, The Herald, The Independent, The Observer, The Scotsman, The Sun, The Sun on Sunday, The Sunday Telegraph, The Sunday Times, The Times, The Mail on Sunday.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of TV and radio stations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use official station names and styling as listed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Channel 4; BBC One, Two, Three, Four; ITV1, ITV2, ITV3; Radio 5 Live.
